title: Goroutines and WaitGroups
summary: Run functions concurrently with go, wait for them with sync.WaitGroup, split work into chunks, and guard shared data with a Mutex.
intro: A goroutine is a function running at the same time as the rest of your program. Go makes them cheap to start and easy to write: one keyword, `go`. This lesson covers starting goroutines and waiting for them with `sync.WaitGroup`, splitting a job into chunks that run at the same time, and protecting shared data with `sync.Mutex` so goroutines never corrupt it.

steps.title: Starting goroutines
steps.body:
Put `go` in front of a function call and that call runs in a new goroutine, a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime. The `go` statement returns right away and `main` keeps going.

```go
go square(i, nums, results, &wg)
```

When `main` returns, the program ends, even if goroutines are still running. Their work is simply lost. So `main` must wait, and `sync.WaitGroup` is the standard tool:

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
wg.Add(1)      // before go, so Wait cannot miss it
go worker(&wg) // inside worker: defer wg.Done()
wg.Wait()      // blocks until every Done has run
```

- Call `wg.Add(1)` in `main` before the `go` statement, never inside the goroutine.
- Start the worker with `defer wg.Done()` so it counts as finished on every return path.
- Pass `*sync.WaitGroup`. A copy has its own counter, so `Done` never reaches the original and `Wait` deadlocks.

The scheduler decides when each goroutine runs, so lines printed inside them can come out in a different order on every run. Give each one its own slot, `results[i]`, and print from `main` after `Wait`. Writes to different elements never collide. A goroutine starts with a stack of a few KB that grows as needed, so starting thousands is cheap.

example.title: Square in goroutines
example.prompt: Read numbers until the input ends, square each one in its own goroutine, wait, and print the results in input order.
example.explanation: `results` has one slot per number, made before any goroutine starts. Each `square` call writes only `results[i]`, so no two goroutines touch the same element. `wg.Add(1)` runs in `main` before each `go`, and every worker calls `wg.Done()` on the way out through `defer`. `main` passes `&wg`, a pointer, so all five `Done` calls lower the same counter. `wg.Wait()` blocks until it reaches zero, and only then does `main` print. The goroutines may finish in any order, but the output is always the same because each value lands at its own index.

practice.title: Word lengths
practice.prompt:
Measure every input word in its own goroutine and print the lengths in the original order.

1. Add `"sync"` to the imports.
2. Write `wordLen(i int, words []string, lengths []int, wg *sync.WaitGroup)`. It defers `wg.Done()` and stores `len(words[i])` in `lengths[i]`.
3. In `main`, declare a `sync.WaitGroup`. For each index, call `wg.Add(1)`, then `go wordLen(i, words, lengths, &wg)`.
4. Call `wg.Wait()` before the print loop, so the lengths are filled in.
5. The starter already reads the words and prints one `word: length` line per word.

Input:

```text
go is fun
```

Expected output:

```text
go: 2
is: 2
fun: 3
```
hints: The worker has the same shape as `square` in the example: `defer wg.Done()` first, then one write to its own index.
Pass `&wg`, not `wg`. A copied WaitGroup never reaches zero in `main`, so `Wait` deadlocks.

steps.title: Splitting work into chunks
steps.body:
For a big job, split the data into chunks and give each chunk its own goroutine. `s[lo:hi]` makes a chunk without copying anything: it is a new slice header that points into the same backing array.

```go
size := len(nums) / NumChunks
for c := 0; c < NumChunks; c++ {
	lo, hi := c*size, (c+1)*size
	wg.Add(1)
	go func(c int, part []int) {
		defer wg.Done()
		// work on part, store the answer in partial[c]
	}(c, nums[lo:hi])
}
```

- An anonymous goroutine passes the loop variable and the chunk as arguments. In Go 1.16 the loop reuses one `c` for every iteration, so a closure that read `c` directly could see a later value. Arguments are copied when the `go` statement runs.
- The closure may still use `wg` and `partial` from `main`. It captures those variables themselves, not copies, so `wg.Done()` reaches the real WaitGroup.
- Each goroutine reads only its own chunk and writes only `partial[c]`, so nothing is shared.
- After `wg.Wait()`, combine the partial results in `main`.

When the length does not divide evenly, let the last chunk take the rest: `if c == NumChunks-1 { hi = len(nums) }`.

example.title: Sum in four chunks
example.prompt: Sum the numbers 1 to 100 with four goroutines of 25 numbers each, then print the partial sums and the total.
example.explanation: `size` is 25, so the chunks are `nums[0:25]`, `nums[25:50]`, `nums[50:75]`, and `nums[75:100]`. Each is a slice header pointing into the same array, so no numbers are copied. The goroutine gets `c` and its chunk as arguments, adds up the chunk in a local `sum`, and writes it once to `partial[c]`. After `wg.Wait()` all four slots are filled, and `main` adds them to get 5050.

practice.title: Chunked maximum
practice.prompt:
Find the largest of 12 numbers with three goroutines that each scan 4 of them.

1. Add `"sync"` to the imports and declare a `sync.WaitGroup`.
2. Loop `c` from 0 while `c < NumChunks`. Compute `lo, hi := c*size, (c+1)*size` and call `wg.Add(1)`.
3. Start `go func(c int, part []int) { ... }(c, nums[lo:hi])`. Inside, defer `wg.Done()`, find the largest value in `part`, and store it in `partial[c]`.
4. After `wg.Wait()`, set `best` to the largest value in `partial`. You can remove the `_ = size` line.
5. Print `partial`, then `Max:` and the overall maximum.

Expected output:

```text
[42 88 73]
Max: 88
```
hints: Copy the example's loop and change only the body of the goroutine: track the largest value instead of a sum.
Start the running maximum at `part[0]`, then compare the rest. Do the same with `partial` after `wg.Wait()`.

steps.title: Mutex for shared data
steps.body:
A data race is two goroutines touching the same memory at once, with at least one of them writing. `n++` looks like one step but is really read, add, write. Two goroutines can both read 41 and both write 42, so a racy counter loses counts and its total can change from run to run. Maps are worse: writing a map while another goroutine reads or writes it, without a lock, can crash the whole program with `fatal error: concurrent map writes`, and `recover` cannot catch it.

A `sync.Mutex` lets only one goroutine at a time into a section of code. Keep it in a `mu` field right next to the data it guards:

```go
type Counter struct {
	mu sync.Mutex
	n  int
}

func (c *Counter) Inc() {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	c.n++
}
```

- `Lock` waits until no one else holds the mutex. `defer c.mu.Unlock()` releases it on every return path, even after a panic.
- Use pointer receivers for every method. A value receiver copies the struct, mutex included, so each call locks its own private copy and guards nothing.
- After `wg.Wait()` every goroutine is finished, so `main` can read the fields safely.

Embedding `sync.Mutex` also works, but it makes `Lock` and `Unlock` part of the type's API, so the course keeps a named `mu` field.

example.title: Safe counter
example.prompt: Increment one shared counter from 100 goroutines and print the final count.
example.explanation: All 100 goroutines call `Inc` on the same `counter`. Inside, `Lock` lets one goroutine at a time run `c.n++`, so no increment is lost and the total is always 100. `Inc` has a pointer receiver, so `counter.Inc()` works on the real struct and its one mutex. The goroutine needs no arguments here because it does not use the loop variable. `main` reads `counter.n` only after `wg.Wait()`, when no goroutine can still be writing.

practice.title: Safe word count
practice.prompt:
Count words with one goroutine per word, using a mutex to guard the shared map.

1. Finish `Inc`: lock `c.mu`, `defer c.mu.Unlock()`, then add 1 to `c.counts[word]`.
2. In `main`, declare a `sync.WaitGroup` and remove the `_ = words` line.
3. For each word, call `wg.Add(1)` and start `go func(w string) { ... }(w)`. Inside, defer `wg.Done()` and call `counter.Inc(w)`.
4. Call `wg.Wait()` before the starter's code that prints the counts in sorted key order.

Expected output:

```text
go: 3
rust: 2
zig: 1
```
hints: `Inc` has the same three lines as the example's `Inc`, with `c.counts[word]++` as the last one.
Pass the word as an argument to the goroutine, because Go 1.16 reuses the range variable for every iteration.

recap:
- `go f(x)` runs `f` in a new goroutine. When `main` returns, the program ends, finished or not.
- `var wg sync.WaitGroup`: `wg.Add(1)` before each `go`, `defer wg.Done()` inside, `wg.Wait()` in `main`.
- Pass `&wg` to named workers. A copied WaitGroup deadlocks.
- Give each goroutine its own index or chunk (`s[lo:hi]`), then combine and print from `main` after `Wait`.
- Pass loop variables to goroutines as arguments: `go func(c int, part []int) { ... }(c, s[lo:hi])`.
- Guard shared data with a `mu sync.Mutex` field: `c.mu.Lock()`, then `defer c.mu.Unlock()`, in pointer-receiver methods.
- Unguarded shared counters lose updates, and unguarded concurrent map writes crash the program.
